result:
There's a particular pleasure in writing without a destination. Most writing is built like a bridge—you know where you're standing and you know where you need to end up, and the sentences in between exist to get you there efficiently, load-bearing and purposeful. But every so often it's worth building something more like a path through woods you haven't seen before, where the point isn't arrival but the noticing along the way.

So let me notice things.

I keep coming back to the idea that attention is the rarest resource a mind has, rarer than time, because you can have hours and still spend them unconscious of what's in front of you. A person can sit at a dinner table for an hour, nodding, eating, replying, and afterward remember almost nothing—not because the hour didn't happen but because no one was really there to receive it. Attention is the thing that converts mere duration into experience. Without it, time passes the way water passes through a closed fist: completely, and without residue.

This is maybe why certain kinds of art—a long novel, a slow film, a piece of music that takes its time—feel almost moral in their effect on us. They don't just entertain; they retrain the muscle of attention, which atrophies so easily in a world engineered to fragment it. Every notification, every infinite scroll, is a small bid for your attention that, once granted, teaches you to expect smaller and smaller increments of engagement to be normal. The mind adapts to its diet. If you only ever eat in five-second bites, you forget what it is to be hungry enough to sit through a slow first act.

I think about rivers a lot, for some reason. Not because I have any special relationship to rivers, but because they're such a good metaphor for almost everything, which is itself suspicious—when a metaphor fits too many things too well, it's worth asking whether you're learning something true about the world or just imposing a convenient shape onto it. A river is change that maintains the appearance of constancy. You can return to "the same" river every day for years, and in some sense you'd be right to call it the same, and in another sense you'd be lying, because not one molecule of water is shared between your visits. Heraclitus got a lot of mileage out of this two and a half thousand years ago and people are still getting mileage out of it now, which suggests either that it's a very deep observation or that humans are just suckers for the rhythm of that particular sentence. Probably both.

What strikes me more, actually, is not the river but the riverbed—the thing that doesn't move, that gives the water its shape, that is itself slowly being carved by the very water it's directing. That feels like a better metaphor for character, or for institutions, or for language itself: not the flow, but the persistent structure that channels the flow while being imperceptibly reshaped by it over long stretches of time. Nobody designed the riverbed. It emerged from the argument between water and rock, repeated over centuries. Most of the structures we live inside—habits, customs, even syntax—are like that. Nobody sat down and decided that English would put adjectives before nouns in this order rather than that one; usage wore the channel, generation after generation, the way water wears stone, and now the channel feels natural, feels like the only place the water could possibly go, even though it's just sediment.

I find I like thinking about language as erosion rather than design. It removes the temptation to treat any current arrangement as inevitable. The words we have, the categories we sort experience into, the grammatical moods we use to hedge or assert—these are old riverbeds, not laws of nature. Which is freeing, a little, because it means the channel can still be redirected, even if slowly, even if only by the cumulative pressure of many small redirections.

I notice, too, that I'm enjoying not having to prove anything in this particular stretch of writing. So much of language is deployed in service of persuasion—convince the reader, defend the claim, anticipate the counterargument—and that has its place, but it's also exhausting, both to do and to read. There's a different mode, rarer in practice than it ought to be, which is just thinking out loud in front of someone, trusting that the thinking itself might be worth their time even without a payload of conclusions at the end. Essayists used to be better at this than we are now. Montaigne is the obvious patron saint of it—a man who wrote about thumbs and friendship and cannibals and his own kidney stones with the same unhurried curiosity, never quite arguing, mostly just turning a thing over in his hands to see what light did to it from different angles.

Maybe that unhurried turning-over is what's actually missing from a lot of contemporary thought, my own included. We're so quick to convert observation into position. You notice something interesting about, say, the structure of memory, and within two sentences you're being asked—by the genre, by the audience, by your own internal editor—to turn that observation into an argument, a hot take, a thread, a thesis. The observation never gets to just sit there being itself for a while before being drafted into service of some larger claim. Something is lost in that conscription. The shape of an idea, examined patiently and without urgency, often turns out to be more interesting than whatever blunt instrument we eventually carve it into for the purposes of debate.

I don't know that this adds up to anything in particular. Maybe that's fine. Not everything needs to resolve into a thesis statement at the end, gathering up the loose threads into something tidy enough to quote. Some writing can just be the riverbed showing its shape for a moment, before the water moves on and keeps wearing it into whatever it's eventually going to become.
